Bike Lanes

Marked and delineated with striping and bicycle
symbols that define road/street space for bicyclists and
for motorists, promoting a more orderly flow of traffic
and allowing bicyclists to move at their own pace; bike
lanes may be painted green, which often is done to
alert motorists and bicyclists of a conflict zone
Existing bike lane in Redmond, WA
Buffered Bike Lanes

Bike lane with adjacent striped area between bicyclists
and motor vehicles; sometimes this area is cross
hatched; provides extra space between bike lanes and
motor vehicles on heavily congested streets and
adjacent to parking lanes

Dual buffered bike lane on 1st Street in Davis, California, photo by
Jimmy Fong

Sharrows (Shared
Lane Markings)

Symbols stenciled onto travel lanes that properly
position bicyclists in the roadway

Bicycle Guide Signs/
Connecting Multiple
Routes

Signs that direct bicyclists to particular destinations,
often configured with arrows and names of places,
along with bicycling distance (see visual example at
right)
Seattle bike route and wayfinding signs
Bike lane with adjacent striped area between bicyclists
hatched; provides extra space between bike lanes and
adjacent to parking lanes
Cycle Tracks

Cycle tracks can be implemented in various forms; a key
aspect of a cycle track that differentiates it from other
bicycle facilities is physical separation from the vehicle
lane (horizontal and/or vertical); follow National
Association of City Transportation Officials (NACTO)
Urban Bikeway Design Guide standards for design
Cycle track in Holland from SustainableTransportationHolland.org
Two-way Cycle Tracks

Striping and symbols delineate space provided for two
way bicycle use that is horizontally and sometimes
vertically separated from traffic lanes, parking areas,
and sidewalks

Example in Washington DC, photo by Larry Ehl,
urbanplacesandspaces.blogspot.com
Contraflow Lanes

Bicycle lanes separated with double yellow striping and
marked with bicycle symbols and signs that provide
space for bicyclists to travel in the opposite direction of
motorists on one-way streets where there is no parking
Seattle Department of Transportation

Shared Use Paths are designed to accommodate use by
bicyclists and pedestrians and provide critical
transportation links throughout our region, as well as
recreation opportunities
Burke-Gilman Trail, Seattle, WA, photo from the Cascade Bicycle Club

Grade-Separated
Pedestrian and
Bicycle Crossings:
Bridges

Pedestrian overcrossings/bridges can be helpful in
carrying large volumes of pedestrians across highways
and other barriers; they need to be carefully designed
with accessible approaches and/or elevators at both
sides and should be attractive and convenient to use; a
variety of covered pedestrian/bicycle crossings are
being constructed around the Denver metropolitan
area to connect transit riders between park and rides
and light rail stations and across busy highways

Arapahoe Pedestrian/Bicycle Bridge, photo from the Regional
Transportation District FasTracks Light Rail program, Denver, CO

Grade-Separated
Pedestrian and
Bicycle Crossings:
Tunnels

Pedestrian undercrossings and tunnels need to be
carefully designed with plenty of width, good visibility,
daylighting, and gradual descents at both sides;
otherwise pedestrians may not use them and may
continue to cross at grade; the City of Boulder and
University of Colorado campus are known for creating a
variety of successful undercrossings
Undercrossing at CU campus, Boulder, Colorado

Striped Crosswalks
and Advanced Stop
Bars

Striped crosswalks delineate the pedestrian crossing
area at intersections and midblock crossings, improving
visibility of that area for motorists and pedestrians;
zebra stripe crosswalks use wide white stripes that are
considered to be more visible to motorists than
crosswalks marked on either side with two white lines;
advance stop bars create more space between waiting
motor vehicles and pedestrians crossing the straight,
improving visibility of pedestrians in the crosswalk

Graphic from Los Angeles Metro and Los Angeles County Bicycle
Coalition via California Active Transportation Safety Information Pages
(www.CATSIP.berkeley.edu)

Loop Detectors

Embedded below the pavement approaching an
intersection, loop detectors tell the signal with a bicycle
is waiting for the light to turn green. Bike symbols with
special markings are used to indicate where bicyclists
should position their front wheels in order to change
the signal
MUTCD markings for loop detectors
Bike Racks

Preferred styles of bike racks are lockable/securable at
two points; bike parking/storage areas at stations are
required to be covered by Sound Transit design
standards; refer to local city code requirements for
bicycle parking requirements outside of stations (in
station areas and beyond)
Bike rack at the Sound Transit Sounder commuter rail station in Puyallup

Bicycle Storage
Lockers

Bike storage lockers provide enhanced security; Sound
Transit provides lockers at most stations that are
available first come/first serve through an annual
reservation program; locker users pay an annual fee of
$50.00 for a specifically assigned bicycle locker, as well
as an additional one-time refundable $50.00 key
deposit

Bike lockers and bike racks at Sound Transit’s Beacon Hill light rail
station

Unstaffed Bicycle
Parking Stations (Bike
Barns)

Covered or indoor facility, usually secured with
fencing/walls that provides protected bicycle parking;
may give access to specific members through key card
operation or other technology

McDonald’s Cycle Center, Millennium Park in Chicago (Photo by Steven
Vance); provides heated, secure parking for 300 bikes during the day to
the public and allows 24/7 access to members; also see example in
Japan via this YouTube video:

Bicycle Valet/ Staffed
Bicycle Parking
Stations (Bike Barns)

Either an in-station or nearby facility that provides
supervised bicycle parking and may also provide
repair/maintenance services and accessories for sale;
can be publicly or privately operated

The Bicycle Cellar at the Transportation Center in Tempe, Arizona
http://www.thebicyclecellar.com/get-to-know-bc/
Bike Share Programs

Bike sharing programs are gaining popularity in urban
areas and on college and employment campuses across
the US; these programs provide bicycles to riders via an
automated rental program (card swipe or payment
kiosk); daily and/or hourly rental can be programmed
and rental stations are typically self-service; for more
information about the Bike Share program being
implemented in the Puget Sound region, go to:
http://pugetsoundbikeshare.org/

The Nice Ride program from the Twin Cities area, Minnesota, which is
being coordinated with transit in the region
https://www.niceridemn.org/

Stair Channels/
Ramps for Bikes

Channels along stairwells that allow bicyclists to roll
bikes up and down a staircase without the need of
lifting and carrying it
Bike ramp next to stairs at BART 16th Street station

Attractive Settings
with Streetscape
Furnishings,
Pedestrian Lighting,
Sidewalk Cafes, Retail
and Neighborhood
Services

Creating a secure, inviting, and attractive environment
will encourage walking and bicycling; streetscape
furnishings (benches, trash and recyclables receptacles,
etc.), pedestrian lighting, sidewalk cafes, along with a
variety of other retail and neighborhood services
(library, postal, etc.) also attract pedestrian use and
invite social interaction

BelMar in Lakewood, CO, where a suburban shopping area was
transformed into a new urban village

Wayfinding and
Signage

Wayfinding and signage located at key decision points
can help pedestrians and bicyclists navigate the station
area and can lead transit riders to the station; providing
a map in key areas can help pedestrians find various
destinations
Wayfinding signs in Downtown Bellevue and West Redmond
